Heritage walk in Pune: Peshwa wadas, caves and hill forts

A heritage walk in Pune usually starts at Shaniwar Wada, the Peshwas' palace of 1732, and goes through the old peths (market quarters) with their wadas, temples and Mahatma Phule's house. Pataleshwar cave, the Aga Khan Palace and the Kelkar Museum add other periods, and forts and Buddhist caves lie within an hour or two.

We arrange heritage walks in Pune and study days to nearby caves and forts on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Pune matters for heritage

For most of the 18th century Pune was the effective capital of the Maratha state, run by the Peshwas, the chief ministers who held power in the name of the Chhatrapatis. It was then a centre of 19th century social reform, education and the national movement. The result is a city whose old core is made of courtyard houses (wadas), neighbourhood temples and schools rather than grand monuments.

Pune also sits at the centre of a much older region. Buddhist caves at Karla, Bhaja and Bedse, rock-cut shrines, and the hill forts that were inscribed in 2025 as part of the Maratha Military Landscapes of India (among them Shivneri, Lohgad and Rajgad near Pune) can all be reached by road. Our guide to forts of India explains how these hill forts worked.

Layers of history in Pune

The earliest dated monuments near Pune are rock-cut Buddhist caves of roughly the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE, on the trade routes that climbed the Western Ghats from the coast. Bhaja and Karla, near Lonavala, have some of the finest early chaitya halls in India. Inside the city, Pataleshwar is a rock-cut Shaiva cave usually dated to around the 8th century CE. Our explainer on Buddhist caves in India sets these in context.

Pune was a small town under the Ahmadnagar and Bijapur sultanates, and a jagir (estate) of Shahaji Bhosale, father of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, who spent part of his childhood at the Lal Mahal here in the 1630s and 1640s. The present Lal Mahal is a modern reconstruction.

In 1720 Bajirao I became Peshwa, and in 1730 to 1732 he built Shaniwar Wada as his seat. The city grew around it in planned peths named after days of the week (Shaniwar, Budhwar, Somwar and so on). After the British defeated the last Peshwa in 1818, Pune became a cantonment and educational city. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls at Bhide Wada in 1848, and the city produced reformers and leaders from Gopal Krishna Gokhale to Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

Places a heritage walk in Pune covers

  1. Shaniwar Wada 1730 to 1732

    Seat of the Peshwas, burnt in 1828. Walls, gates such as Dilli Darwaza, and foundations survive.

  2. Lal Mahal Modern reconstruction of a 1630s house

    Marks the site of the house where Shivaji spent part of his boyhood; read it as memory, not original fabric.

  3. Kasba Ganpati 17th century

    Neighbourhood temple considered the city's presiding Ganesha; one of the oldest shrines in the peths.

  4. Vishrambaug Wada Early 19th century

    Built for the last Peshwa, Bajirao II; the carved wooden facade is the best surviving example in the city.

  5. Tulshibaug Ram Mandir 18th century

    Temple complex in a busy market, with a tall shikhara added later.

  6. Bhide Wada 1848 school site

    Where the Phules opened a school for girls; a memorial is being developed on the site.

  7. Mahatma Phule Wada 19th century

    Home of Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule in Ganj Peth, now a memorial.

  8. Nana Wada 1780

    Built by Nana Phadnavis, the Peshwas' minister; later used as a school.

  9. Pataleshwar Cave About 8th century CE

    Rock-cut Shaiva cave with a Nandi pavilion cut from the same rock.

  10. Parvati Hill 1749 onward

    Peshwa temple complex on a hill with a view over the city; a long stair climb.

  11. Shinde Chhatri 1794

    Memorial to Mahadji Shinde, mixing Rajasthani and Maratha styles.

  12. Aga Khan Palace 1892

    Where Gandhi, Kasturba and Mahadev Desai were held in 1942 to 1944; Kasturba and Desai's samadhis are here.

  13. Sinhagad Fort Medieval, famous for the 1670 battle

    Hill fort south-west of the city linked to Tanaji Malusare; vehicle needed.

  14. Karla and Bhaja Caves About 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE

    Early Buddhist chaitya halls and viharas near Lonavala; vehicle needed.

Walking routes in Pune

Peshwa Pune on foot

About 3 hours

Shaniwar Wada → Lal Mahal → Kasba Ganpati → Nana Wada → Vishrambaug Wada → Tulshibaug Ram Mandir

Reformers' Pune

About 2.5 hours, with a short drive

Bhide Wada → Mahatma Phule Wada → Aga Khan Palace

Caves and forts (vehicle needed)

A full day

Pataleshwar Cave → Sinhagad Fort → Karla and Bhaja Caves

Museums in Pune

  • Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum. A private collection of everyday objects: lamps, nutcrackers, musical instruments, textiles and a reconstructed wada interior.
  • Deccan College Museum of Archaeology. University museum with prehistoric tools, excavated pottery and the Maratha history museum; check access before visiting.
  • Aga Khan Palace Museum. Photographs and objects on the national movement and Gandhi's detention.
  • Mahatma Phule Museum. A 19th century museum building on Shivajinagar with natural history and industrial collections.

Best time for a walk

October to February for walks and forts. The monsoon makes the forts and caves green but paths slippery; the old city walk is fine year round in early mornings.

What you see on a Pune heritage walk

The old city walk reads a wada: the outer wall and gate, the chowk (courtyard), the wooden pillars and brackets, and the way families, servants and business shared the space. Shaniwar Wada was largely destroyed by fire in 1828, so only the fortification walls, gates and foundations survive, but these are still the best place to explain the layout. Nearby Vishrambaug Wada keeps its carved wooden front.

From there the route moves through temples such as Kasba Ganpati and Tulshibaug Ram Mandir, the market lanes of Budhwar and Raviwar peths, and the site of Bhide Wada. Mahatma Phule Wada in Ganj Peth, the Phules' home, completes the story of reform. A heritage photography walk works well in these lanes, with students recording carved brackets, doorways and inscriptions as evidence.

Pataleshwar cave, on Jangli Maharaj Road across the river, is a short drive and lets you show a rock-cut shrine without leaving the city. The lecture on rock-cut sacred architecture is a natural preparation.

Planning a Pune heritage walk for schools and groups

The old city route is about 2 to 3 kilometres on level streets, suitable for classes 4 and above. Traffic is heavy after 10 am, so start early; Sunday mornings are best. Shaniwar Wada and Aga Khan Palace are ASI or government-run sites with timings and tickets, so check before you go.

Forts and caves need a vehicle and a separate day. Sinhagad, about 35 kilometres south-west, involves a drive to the top and short walks. Karla and Bhaja involve stair climbs of a few hundred steps. Talaash Heritage does not currently run a fixed Pune programme, so we build each trip on request: our study tour built for your group can combine the old city, the caves and the forts, and the Mumbai caves, city and living traditions journey extends naturally to Pune and Karla.

Questions people ask

What are the main historical places in Pune?

Shaniwar Wada, Lal Mahal, Vishrambaug Wada, Kasba Ganpati, Parvati Hill, Pataleshwar Cave, Phule Wada, Shinde Chhatri and the Aga Khan Palace in the city, with Sinhagad Fort and the Karla and Bhaja caves nearby.

What happened to Shaniwar Wada?

It was built by Peshwa Bajirao I in 1730 to 1732 and burnt in a fire in 1828, after the British took Pune. The massive outer walls, gates and the foundations of the inner buildings survive and are protected by the ASI.

Are there UNESCO sites near Pune?

Yes. Shivneri, Lohgad and Rajgad near Pune are among the 12 forts inscribed in 2025 as the Maratha Military Landscapes of India. Ajanta and Ellora are further away, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar.

Is a Pune heritage walk good for school students?

Yes. The Peshwa walk is flat and compact. Students can study wada plans, temple layouts and the reform movement in one morning. Forts and caves make a second day for older classes.

Which museums in Pune are good for history?

The Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum for everyday objects and crafts, the Deccan College museum for archaeology and Maratha history, and the Aga Khan Palace for the national movement.
